summary:
LUNAPOLE answers two questions for any candidate lunar south-pole site: when is the Sun actually above the local horizon, and when is Earth visible?

It does not use a flat map. For each site it marches 720 horizon rays across a 25 km LOLA elevation crop, including lunar curvature, and builds a measured horizon profile at 0.5° azimuth steps. It then samples a full year and reports how much of the span is lit, the longest continuous dark run with its start date, and the direct-to-Earth window — alongside a 3D terrain view, an illumination and Earth-visibility pole-cap map, and a scrubbable sky panorama.

Four contrasting sites ship in the demo: Shackleton, de Gerlache, Haworth and Nobile, each labelled as an IAU feature centre rather than a landing site.

Everything is precomputed into a static app, so it runs with no network on a laptop or phone. Power and communications decide every south-pole mission concept; this lets planners compare sites and seasons in one view.
details:
What it does

LUNAPOLE is an offline planning tool for the lunar south pole. Pick a site and it tells you when the Sun clears the real, measured horizon and when Earth is above it — the two facts that decide solar power and direct-to-Earth communications for a lander.

How it works

For each site we take the LOLA gridded elevation product (10 m/px inside 87.5°S, 20 m/px out to 80°S) and crop a 25 km disc around the site. From the site pixel we march 720 azimuth rays at 10 m steps, subtract the lunar curvature drop (259 m at 30 km), and keep the maximum elevation angle per bin. That gives a 720-bin horizon profile — the local skyline, not an idealised sphere.

Against that profile we propagate the Sun and Earth with NASA NAIF SPICE (DE440s planetary ephemeris, moon_pa_de440 lunar orientation, leapseconds and body constants). Sub-solar and sub-Earth directions are computed in the Moon-fixed frame, so libration and the 1.54° axial tilt are handled rather than approximated. We sample a full year at 60-minute steps (8,767 samples per site) and report the fraction of the span with any part of the solar disc above the horizon, the longest continuous dark run and when it starts, and Earth any-limb and full-disc visibility.

The app has four linked panels: a 3D terrain view with the Sun and Earth placed on the reconstructed skyline; an illumination and Earth-visibility map of the whole pole cap; a 0–360° panorama of measured horizon versus Sun elevation; and a scrubbable year timeline. One click turns all of it into a two-sentence verdict that names the measured numbers.

Benefits and impact

Mission planners, educators and the public can compare sites and seasons in seconds instead of reading tables. Because the horizon is measured from real topography, the tool reproduces the effect that matters most at the pole: a site 1.5 km up a crater wall can be lit for a quarter of the year while the floor beside it is never lit at all. In our bake, Shackleton's centre is lit 27.8% of the span with a 511-hour continuous dark run, de Gerlache's centre is never lit, and Nobile keeps a direct-to-Earth limb 37.1% of the time. Those contrasts are the planning conversation.

Tools and languages

Python for the science pipeline (NumPy, GDAL for the JPEG 2000 elevation products, SpiceyPy for ephemerides). The front end is plain ES modules plus one vendored copy of three.js — no framework, no build step, no network calls at runtime. Playwright drives the automated panel and latency checks, and a verifier suite gates the build: byte-identical rebake, ephemeris cross-check against JPL Horizons, and DEM sanity checks.

What is creative about it

The interesting move was refusing to draw a shadow map and instead measuring a skyline. Every number in the app is traceable to one DEM pixel and one azimuth bin, and the app says so. We also made the honesty visible: the UI states that each catalogue entry is an IAU feature centre — not a landing site, and not the rim peak that published illumination figures describe.

Factors we considered

Time and reproducibility: everything is baked ahead of the demo so the app runs offline on a phone. Uncertainty: ephemeris accuracy is verified to 0.0076° against JPL Horizons; horizon accuracy is limited by DEM resolution (10 vs 20 m/px) and by the 25 km crop, and both limits are stated in the app. Scope: four sites instead of six, chosen for contrast.

Limitations we state on screen

The illumination span is labelled as 365.25 days and explicitly not the 18.6-year precession cycle. Map pixels are coarser (320 m) than the per-site horizon march. The map is known to be optimistic on low-horizon pixels.
